Abstract
Training in mindfulness, classically described as a receptive attentiveness to present events
and experiences, has been shown to improve attention and working memory. Both are key
to long-term memory formation, and the present three-study series used multiple methods
to examine whether mindfulness would enhance episodic memory, a key form of long-term
memory. In Study 1 (N = 143), a self-reported state of mindful attention predicted better rec-
ognition performance in the Remember-Know (R-K) paradigm. In Study 2 ( N = 93), very
brief training in a focused attention form of mindfulness also produced better recognition
memory performance on the R-K task relative to a randomized, well-matched active control
condition. Study 3 (N = 57) extended these findings by showing that relative to randomized
active and inactive control conditions the effect of very brief mindfulness training general-
ized to free-recall memory performance. This study also found evidence for mediation of the
mindfulness training— episodic memory relation by intrinsic motivation. These findings indi-
cate that mindful attention can beneficially impact motivation and episodic memory, with
potential implications for educational and occupational performance.
Introduction
Mental time travel is a hallmark of human subjectivity, a key feature of which is the capacity to
consciously re-experience past events. This episodic memory, the remembrance of past episodes
from specific times and places, allows humans to guide their present and anticipated future
behavior. By influencing what information is placed in working memory, episodic memory
allows us to apply knowledge about our past to execute current tasks and to reflect on, plan for,
and derive preferences for future situations [ 1]. A form of long-term memory, and specifically

Limitations and future research
Like much previous research in this area, these studies were conducted with university student samples, and tests of the generalizability of the results to other populations, such as older adults or less educated samples, are needed. Also, because we did not measure or otherwise control for participant expectancy effects on the outcomes, we cannot definitively conclude that expectancies did not bear some influence on the study results. There are reasons to believe that expectancy is not a likely alternative explanation for the condition differences found, including the fact that participants had no prior knowledge of the study hypotheses or procedures, and the audio instructions bore no resemblance to, nor referred to any elements of the task that followed, nor its outcomes. However, in future selecting active control interventions and outcome measures based on prior, independent assessments of expectations could help to rule out expectancy effects [
79
].

humans and other mammals, event memories are imprecise until the emergence of episodic or episodic-like memory during childhood. The onset of episodic-like memory has historically been associated with maturation of the hippocampus, yet the specific neurobiological mechanisms underlying episodic-like memory development are poorly understood. Using mice, we identified a series of cellular and molecular events in the neurodevelopment of the hippocampus that underlies the ontogeny of precise, episodic-like memories. We found that hippocampus-dependent memories increase in precision at the beginning of the fourth postnatal week (i.e., between postnatal days 20 and 24), following a transient period of elevated neuronal activity in hippocampal subfield CA1. The emergence of precise, episodic-like memories during the fourth postnatal week involves a shift in excitatory-inhibitory balance in CA1 that is initiated by the formation of the extracellular matrix around parvalbumin (PV+)-expressing interneurons. The maturation of CA1 PV+ interneurons by extracellular perineuronal nets (PNNs) subsequently allows experiences encoded by older mice to be allocated to sparse neuronal engram ensembles that support precise, episodic-like memories. Lastly, we found that the development of CA1 PNNs and episodic-like memory precision is regulated by early-life experiences, rather than chronological age alone. Specifically, episodic-like memory development can be decelerated by adverse experiences or accelerated by enriching experiences occurring during the early postnatal period. In summary, the research contained in this thesis demonstrates that the development of episodic-like memory requires adult-like neuronal allocation mechanisms that are controlled by the maturation of the extracellular matrix surrounding inhibitory circuitry in CA1. The timing of this shift in hippocampal function is shaped by early-life experiences, suggesting that the hippocampus undergoes a sensitive period for the emergence of episodic-like memories.\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "10a2832f8c0be126091eb2a48b3b3de6e0663eaf56d04f24f784bc9f6452666f", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_formed_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0153309", "doi:10.1016/b978-0-12-809324-5.21051-1", "openalex:W2342933773", "openalex:W2591137108", "openalex:W1553276161", "openalex:W7132983942"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0153309", "https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0153309&type=printable", "https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-12-809324-5.21051-1", "https://era.ed.ac.uk/bitstreams/b34f3d29-6986-4092-be79-596a84d20101/download"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+of+preference+formation+in+reinforcement+learning+from+human+feedback+RLHF+and+long-term+memory&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6928698\", \"title\": [\"Human Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback: Feedback Mechanisms, Meta-Collaborative Monitoring, and Identity Positioning in Long-Term Human-AI Collaboration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper proposes the concept of \\\"Human Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback\\\" (Human-RLAIF) to describe how long-term interaction with generative AI may shape users' behavior and cognition within an evolving feedback environment. Drawing on the researcher's own collaboration records with a conversational AI system (a full-trajectory corpus of 1,611 conversation windows and 25,859 messages, of which 1,489 conversation windows and 24,304 messages constitute the primary coding corpus), this study adopts an exploratory longitudinal self-case-study design and identifies several possible patterns through thematic coding and aggregated trend analysis: (1) questioning strategies shift from direct answerseeking toward requests for structure, archiving, and longer-term rules; (2) the user side shows early signs of a reorganization of collaborative labor, while AI responses increasingly provide elaboration, organization, and scaffolding; (3) the user side exhibits more behaviors aimed at governing the collaboration itself, such as requesting risk reminders, reality checks, and explicit collaboration boundaries; and (4) identity-related change currently appears only as preliminary signs of shifts in identity positioning and role-based perspective-taking, which is insufficient to claim that stable identity transformation has occurred. The paper also discusses long-term risks associated with AI feedback, including confirmation dependence, pseudo-internalization, identity preemption, and the potential homogenization of expression and cognition. The claims advanced here are exploratory and mechanism-generating rather than statistically demonstrative or causally identificatory. To reduce privacy risks and case-specific narrative distortion, the main text relies on anonymized fragment types, coding labels, and necessary explanation rather than identifiable verbatim dialogue.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6928698\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6338238\", \"title\": [\"The Role of Foundational Autoraters in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)&nbsp;\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The advent of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems has fundamentally transformed diverse fields, including education, healthcare, and natural language processing. A particularly influential area within AI is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which leverages human guidance to optimize learning processes and improve model performance. In this context, foundational autoraters serve as critical tools that automate the evaluation of written submissions, providing essential feedback that guides the learning trajectory of AI models. This abstract explores the significance of foundational autoraters in the RLHF paradigm, focusing on their design, functionalities, and the implications they hold for enhancing AI systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6338238\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.7753/ijcatr1506.1001\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Multimodal LLM Alignment: A Comprehensive Review\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.7753/ijcatr1506.1001\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 5, 20]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.36227/techrxiv.175382817.74693578/v1\", \"title\": [\"Fairness-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (Fair-RLHF): Mitigating Bias in Human Preferences\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Offline Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback aims to train AI agents using predefined human data, however human feedback can be biased which can lead to unfair or sub-optimal decision-making. In this paper, we propose Fairness-Aware Offline RLHF (Fair-RLHF), a framework designed to integrate fairness constraints into Offline Reinforcement Learning. We aim to detect and mitigate bias in Human Feedback. This is done using causal graphs (DAGs), which help in analyzing and identifying where bias originates. This visual representation of the cause-effect relationship determines unfair dependencies and uses fairness techniques to remove them. Furthermore, fairness constraints are applied that use Pareto efficacy to balance fairness with performance, achieving the precision of 46. 5% and 84%. It is optimized by ensuring fairness and maximizing performance. This work provides a fair and efficient RLHF model that aims to bridge the gap between reinforcement learning, fairness constraints, and human feedback by developing a framework that ensures AI agents are unbiased and demographic disparities are reduced.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175382817.74693578/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 7, 29]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "4b8e411b19136c2f1afc3b716c3d396e716ca870c76ab77740df40f73fd051c2", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_formed_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6928698", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6338238", "doi:10.7753/ijcatr1506.1001", "doi:10.36227/techrxiv.175382817.74693578/v1"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6928698", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6338238", "https://doi.org/10.7753/ijcatr1506.1001", "https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175382817.74693578/v1"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
